clinicalPearls: Leprosy is a chronic infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium leprae, with manifestations largely confined to skin, peripheral nerves, eyes, and the upper respiratory tract; M. leprae has a predilection for peripheral nerves (p.1404).

Diagnosis rests on three cardinal signs, of which at least one establishes the diagnosis: (1) a hypopigmented or erythematous skin lesion with definite loss/impairment of sensation, (2) involvement of peripheral nerves shown by definite thickening with sensory impairment, and (3) a positive result for acid-fast bacilli on slit-skin smear or biopsy, or a positive biopsy PCR (p.1409-1410).
The differing immune responses to M. leprae produce a clinical spectrum; immunologic resistance is strong at the tuberculoid end and weakest at the lepromatous end (p.1404, p.1406).
Skin surfaces in tuberculoid lesions are dry, hairless, and anaesthetic owing to destruction of underlying cutaneous nerves, plus autonomic damage causing loss of sweating (p.1407).
Slit-skin smear bacteriologic index runs from negative (tuberculoid) up to 4+ to 6+ with globi (lepromatous), and falls an average of ~1 log unit per year on multidrug therapy (p.1404, p.1407-1408).

Leprosy is the principal treatable cause of peripheral neuropathy worldwide in some settings; nerve enlargement is often palpable (e.g., greater auricular, ulnar, median, radial, lateral popliteal, posterior tibial, sural, superficial peroneal) (p.1409-1410).

Treatment principle: WHO-recommended multidrug therapy (a combination of rifampin, dapsone, and clofazimine) is the standard of care and cures the disease; paucibacillary disease uses two drugs and multibacillary disease uses three, with the cure rate ~99% (no doses given here) (p.1410, p.1412).
M. leprae has never been grown in artificial media; it is propagated only in animal models (mouse footpad, armadillo), which underlies the difficulty of culture-based diagnosis (p.1404).
harrison.pathophysiology: Leprosy is caused by Mycobacterium leprae, an obligate intracellular, acid-fast, rod-shaped bacterium with a preferred growth temperature of 27-30 degrees C, explaining its predilection for cooler surface tissues (skin, peripheral nerves, testes, upper airways) and relative sparing of inner viscera. After entry (assumed mainly via the respiratory tract, sometimes through damaged skin), the pathogenic process usually begins in peripheral nerves once bacilli are engulfed by Schwann cells. The histopathologic outcome - and thus the type of leprosy - depends on the host cell-mediated immune (CMI) response. The Ridley-Jopling spectrum (TT, BT, BB, BL, LL, with indeterminate IL as an early form) reflects this: at the tuberculoid pole, strong CMI produces epithelioid/giant-cell granulomas that destroy nerves (causing anaesthesia and muscle weakness) but contain few bacilli; toward the lepromatous pole, weak CMI permits unrestricted multiplication of bacilli within macrophages (lepra cells) as clumps/globi, with widespread dissemination and high bacterial load. Tissue damage is largely due to delayed hypersensitivity. M. leprae carries the species-specific phenolic glycolipid PGL-1, used in serodiagnosis. M. lepromatosis is a related species associated with diffuse leprosy of Lucio and Latapi.
additionalDifferentials: Hypopigmented macules: pityriasis alba, vitiligo, progressive macular hypomelanosis, pityriasis versicolor, pityriasis rosea, postinflammatory hypopigmentation, sarcoidosis, post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis, morphea (p.1410)

Plaque/nodular lesions: granuloma annulare, cutaneous sarcoidosis, cutaneous leishmaniasis, lupus miliaris disseminatus faciei, nodular histiocytosis, lupus erythematosus, cutaneous T-cell lymphomas (especially mycosis fungoides), secondary syphilis (p.1410)
ENL (type 2 reaction) lesions: erythema nodosum of other etiologies, nodular vasculitis, cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa (p.1410)
Acute-onset polyneuropathy: Guillain-Barre syndrome, toxic polyneuropathy (p.1410)
nonInfectiousMimics: Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, especially mycosis fungoides (p.1410)
additionalInvestigations: Slit-skin smear from standard sites (right earlobe, forehead, chin, and left buttock/upper thigh), Ziehl-Neelsen stained, graded by bacteriologic index (0-6) and microbiologic index (p.1410)
Skin biopsy to confirm diagnosis, classify disease, support diagnosis of reactions, and assess cure; immunochemical staining for M. leprae antigens aids detection of early lesions (p.1410)

PCR / gene amplification (conventional, RT-PCR, multiplex targeting RLEP, 16S rRNA, SodA, antigen genes) - useful in bacteriologic-index-negative cases and for subclinical infection in contacts (p.1410)
PGL-1 antibody testing (ELISA, ML flow lateral-flow assay, UPC-LFA) - more often positive in multibacillary than paucibacillary disease (p.1410)
Lepromin (Mitsuda) skin test - measures cellular immunity; negative in LL/BL leprosy (p.1410)

Nerve function assessment: Semmes-Weinstein monofilament (or WHO-recommended ballpoint pen) touch testing, voluntary muscle testing, nerve conduction studies, and ultrasound of peripheral nerves (p.1410-1411)
redFlags: Type 1 (reversal) reaction: delayed-hypersensitivity reaction with sudden upgrading of CMI; acute swelling and redness of existing lesions, painful/tender nerves with neuritis; can cause silent neuritis and irreversible sensory/motor nerve damage - a medical urgency to prevent disability (p.1407, p.1408-1409)

Type 2 reaction / erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL): immune-complex-mediated syndrome with crops of painful red nodules, fever, malaise, and possible neuritis, iridocyclitis, orchitis, nephritis/renal failure, and (late) amyloidosis (p.1408-1409)

Neuritis with nerve function impairment, including 'silent neuritis' (progressive sensory/motor loss without pain or tenderness) - requires prompt treatment to avoid permanent disability and blindness (p.1409, p.1410-1411)
Lucio's phenomenon in diffuse leprosy of Lucio and Latapi: vasculitis and thrombosis causing hemorrhagic skin infarction and necrotic ulcers (p.1409)
Eye involvement (corneal anaesthesia, iridocyclitis, lagophthalmos, corneal ulceration) threatening sight (p.1408)
harrison.prognosis: Leprosy can be cured effectively: the cure rate with multidrug therapy is ~99% and treatment-failure rates are very low when therapy is completed. Relapse rates are well below 1% except in patients with a very high baseline bacillary load (bacteriologic index >=4), and relapses usually occur within 5 years of finishing therapy; antimicrobial resistance is rare, so relapsed multibacillary patients can be re-treated with the same regimen. The major determinant of long-term outcome is nerve damage and resulting disability, which drives stigma and social exclusion. Highest risk of (additional) nerve damage is in multibacillary patients with nerve impairment already present at diagnosis (up to ~65%); intermediate risk (~16%) in multibacillary patients without impairment or paucibacillary patients with impairment at diagnosis; and lowest (~3%) in paucibacillary patients without impairment. Leprosy reactions and new nerve damage can occur even after completing therapy, up to 3 years afterward. Cure (cessation of bacterial activity) must be distinguished from sequelae (nerve impairment, reactions, disabilities such as claw hand or neuropathic foot) that may persist and require chronic care.
pitfalls: Leprosy is frequently diagnosed late - in non-endemic countries it is often misdiagnosed simply because it is not considered - increasing the risk of irreversible nerve damage and disability (p.1404, p.1410)

On the face, sensory impairment may be difficult to demonstrate because of generous bilateral sensory innervation, which can compensate for damage to certain nerve branches and obscure the indeterminate stage (p.1407, p.1409)

'Silent neuritis' / 'quiet nerve paralysis': nerve function can be lost progressively without pain, paresthesia, tenderness, or other signs of reaction - regular nerve function assessment is needed during and after therapy (p.1409, p.1411)

Distinguishing relapse from a type 1 reaction in paucibacillary disease can be difficult; a therapeutic glucocorticoid trial helps - improvement within 4 weeks favors T1R, lack of response favors relapse (p.1412)

Patients often equate cure with absence of symptoms, but in leprosy bacteriologic cure does not eliminate established nerve-impairment sequelae - this must be explained at completion of therapy (p.1412-1413)
Multidrug therapy for clinical leprosy has apparently not interrupted transmission, and subclinical/undiagnosed multibacillary cases are likely a main source of ongoing spread (p.1405)
harrison.severityClassification: Ridley-Jopling classification (1962) defines five overlapping categories along the immunologic spectrum: tuberculoid (TT), borderline tuberculoid (BT), mid-borderline (BB), borderline lepromatous (BL), and lepromatous (LL), with indeterminate leprosy (IL) as an early form; immunologic resistance is strongest at TT and weakest at LL, with TT and LL relatively stable and BT/BB/BL unstable. For operational/treatment purposes the WHO simplified classification is used: paucibacillary disease = negative slit-skin smears at all sites (or, on clinical criteria, one to five skin lesions and no/only one involved nerve), and multibacillary disease = positive smear at any site (or six or more lesions and/or more than one involved nerve). The WHO disability grading system scores eyes, hands, and feet (grades 0-2), summed into the Eye-Hand-Foot (EHF) score as an overall impairment indicator (p.1405-1406).
management: WHO multidrug therapy combining rifampicin, dapsone and clofazimine, tailored to paucibacillary versus multibacillary classification
Prompt treatment of lepra reactions: corticosteroids for type 1 (reversal) reactions and neuritis, and corticosteroids, clofazimine or thalidomide for type 2 erythema nodosum leprosum
Regular nerve-function assessment with sensory and motor testing, and corticosteroids for acute neuritis to prevent nerve damage and disability
Protection of anaesthetic hands and feet with footwear, wound and ulcer care, and ophthalmic review for ocular involvement
Physiotherapy, occupational therapy and reconstructive surgery for established deformity and disability
Contact tracing, examination of household contacts and single-dose rifampicin post-exposure prophylaxis
Screen for glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency before dapsone and monitor for drug-induced haemolysis and other toxicity
